claims.evidence: This is supported by Rhodopsin immunostaining images shown in Figure 3E, panels c.

claims.claim: The number of dead cells in the ONL was much higher in KitWps/Wps retinas (44 ± 9, n = 10) compared to Kit+/+ retinas (22 ± 7 per section, n = 10) after light damage.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3E (panels D) and 3G, although dead cells were present in the ONL of Kit+/+ retinas (22 ± 7 per section, n = 10), their number was much higher in KitWps/Wps retinas (44 ± 9, n = 10).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay images and quantification shown in Figure 3E,G.

claims.claim: After excessive light exposure, the photoreceptor cells of KitWps/Wps mice are structurally and functionally impaired to a greater extent than those of Kit+/+ mice.
claims.source: Hence, these data show that after excessive light exposure, the photoreceptor cells of KitWps/Wps mice are not only structurally but also functionally impaired to a greater extent than those of Kit+/+ mice.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on the ERG, histological, and TUNEL data presented in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The KitWps mutation accelerates photoreceptor degeneration during light damage.
claims.source: The findings indicate that the KitWps mutation accelerates photoreceptor degeneration during LD.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data showing greater structural and functional impairment in KitWps/Wps mice compared to Kit+/+ mice after light damage.

claims.claim: Fourteen days after AAV8-CMV-GFP virus infection, GFP was found in nearly the entire retina.
claims.source: Fourteen days after virus infection, fundus photographs showed that GFP was found in nearly the entire retina, and cross-sections showed strong GFP signals in photoreceptor cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fundus photographs and cross-section images shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Cross-sections showed strong GFP signals in photoreceptor cells fourteen days after AAV8-CMV-GFP virus infection.
claims.source: Fourteen days after virus infection, fundus photographs showed that GFP was found in nearly the entire retina, and cross-sections showed strong GFP signals in photoreceptor cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cross-section images shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Two weeks after AAV8-KITL infection, western blots showed a significantly increased expression of KITL (3.3 ± 0.46 fold over uninjected control, n = 4).
claims.source: Two weeks after infection, we isolated the neural retinas and examined them for KITL expression. Western blots showed a significantly increased expression of KITL (3.3 ± 0.46 fold over uninjected control, n = 4) (Figure 4B), and immunostaining showed that overexpression of KITL was almost entirely restricted to photoreceptors in the retinas (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Overexpression of KITL was almost entirely restricted to photoreceptors in the retinas after AAV8-KITL infection.
claims.source: Two weeks after infection, we isolated the neural retinas and examined them for KITL expression. Western blots showed a significantly increased expression of KITL (3.3 ± 0.46 fold over uninjected control, n = 4) (Figure 4B), and immunostaining showed that overexpression of KITL was almost entirely restricted to photoreceptors in the retinas (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Without light damage, neither AAV8 nor AAV8-KITL caused detectable changes of retinal morphology in albino mice.
claims.source: Without LD, neither AAV8 (schematically shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) nor AAV8-KITL caused detectable changes of retinal morphology in these mice (Figure 4D,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 4D,E.

claims.claim: After 3 days of light damage treatment, retinas infected by AAV8-KITL were thicker than those infected by control AAV8 or left uninfected.
claims.source: After 3 days of LD treatment, retinas infected by AAV8-KITL were thicker than those infected by control AAV8 or left uninfected (Figure 4D,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 4D,E.

claims.claim: Infection with AAV8 control or AAV8-KITL virus did not cause photoreceptor cell death under normal light conditions.
claims.source: Furthermore, TUNEL analysis showed that infection with AAV8 control or AAV8-KITL virus did not cause photoreceptor cell death under normal light conditions, but under LD conditions, photoreceptor cell death was less pronounced when AAV8-KITL was used (9 ± 1.6%, n = 6) compared to when control AAV8 was used (40.8 ± 4.5%, n = 6) or the eyes were left uninfected (37.7 ± 5%, n = 6) (Figure 4F,G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay images and quantification shown in Figure 4F,G.

claims.claim: Under light damage conditions, photoreceptor cell death was less pronounced when AAV8-KITL was used (9 ± 1.6%, n = 6) compared to when control AAV8 was used (40.8 ± 4.5%, n = 6) or the eyes were left uninfected (37.7 ± 5%, n = 6).
claims.source: Furthermore, TUNEL analysis showed that infection with AAV8 control or AAV8-KITL virus did not cause photoreceptor cell death under normal light conditions, but under LD conditions, photoreceptor cell death was less pronounced when AAV8-KITL was used (9 ± 1.6%, n = 6) compared to when control AAV8 was used (40.8 ± 4.5%, n = 6) or the eyes were left uninfected (37.7 ± 5%, n = 6) (Figure 4F,G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay images and quantification shown in Figure 4F,G.

claims.claim: Overexpression of KITL prevents light-induced photoreceptor degeneration in Kit wild type mice.
claims.source: Taken together, these data indicate that overexpression of KITL prevents light-induced photoreceptor degeneration in Kit wild type mice.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on the histological and TUNEL data presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: After 3 days of light damage treatment, the retinas in both Kit+/+ albino and KitWps/Wps albino mice showed reduced thickness and near-absence of outer segments, but the effects were more severe in KitWps/Wps albino compared with Kit+/+ albino mice.
claims.source: After 3 days of LD treatment, the retinas in both Kit+/+ albino and KitWps/Wps albino mice showed reduced thickness and near-absence of outer segments, but the effects were more severe in KitWps/Wps albino compared with Kit+/+ albino mice (Figure 4H,I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 4H,I.

claims.claim: Injection of the AAV8-KITL virus prevented light-induced reduction of retinal thickness in Kit+/+ albino mice but not in KitWps/Wps albino mice.
claims.source: Importantly, injection of the AAV8-KITL virus prevented light-induced reduction of retinal thickness in Kit+/+ albino mice but not in KitWps/Wps albino mice (Figure 4H,I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 4H,I.

claims.claim: TUNEL assays showed a cell death rate of 40.6 ± 8.2% in Kit+/+ albino mice and 78 ± 11.4% in KitWps/Wps albino mice (n = 4) after control infection.
claims.source: Consistent with these results, TUNEL assays showed a cell death rate of 40.6 ± 8.2% in Kit+/+ albino mice and 78 ± 11.4% in KitWps/Wps albino mice (n = 4) after control infection, while infection with AAV8-KITL significantly reduced the death rate of photoreceptor cells to 8.9 ± 2.1% in Kit+/+ albino mice but not in KitWps/Wps albino mice, where it remained high (75.9 ± 8.2%, n = 4) (Figure 4H,J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay images and quantification shown in Figure 4H,J.

claims.claim: Infection with AAV8-KITL significantly reduced the death rate of photoreceptor cells to 8.9 ± 2.1% in Kit+/+ albino mice but not in KitWps/Wps albino mice, where it remained high (75.9 ± 8.2%, n = 4).
claims.source: Consistent with these results, TUNEL assays showed a cell death rate of 40.6 ± 8.2% in Kit+/+ albino mice and 78 ± 11.4% in KitWps/Wps albino mice (n = 4) after control infection, while infection with AAV8-KITL significantly reduced the death rate of photoreceptor cells to 8.9 ± 2.1% in Kit+/+ albino mice but not in KitWps/Wps albino mice, where it remained high (75.9 ± 8.2%, n = 4) (Figure 4H,J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay images and quantification shown in Figure 4H,J.

claims.claim: Overexpression of KITL can prevent photoreceptor cell death from light damage through activation of the receptor KIT.
claims.source: Collectively, these data suggest that overexpression of KITL can prevent photoreceptor cell death from LD through activation of the receptor KIT.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that AAV8-KITL protects Kit+/+ but not KitWps/Wps mice from light-induced photoreceptor cell death.

claims.claim: At 2 weeks after injection of AAV8-RPE65-KITL, overexpression of KITL was prominent in the RPE (12.1 ± 2.4 fold, n = 4).
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5C and D, at 2 weeks after injection of AAV8-RPE65-KITL, overexpression of KITL was prominent in the RPE (12.1 ± 2.4 fold, n = 4), but its protective effect against LD was very limited (Figure 5E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claims.claim: Overexpression of KITL in RPE has a very limited protective effect against light damage.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5C and D, at 2 weeks after injection of AAV8-RPE65-KITL, overexpression of KITL was prominent in the RPE (12.1 ± 2.4 fold, n = 4), but its protective effect against LD was very limited (Figure 5E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 5E,F.

claims.claim: The death rate of photoreceptor cells was 26.6 ± 5%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RPE65-Flag and only slightly reduced to 21.7 ± 2.8%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RPE65-KITL.
claims.source: In fact, the death rate of photoreceptor cells was 26.6 ± 5%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RPE65-Flag and only slightly reduced to 21.7 ± 2.8%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RPE65-KITL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-a and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay images and quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-a and B.

claims.claim: Overexpression of KITL in RPE does not play a major role in prevention of light-induced photoreceptor degeneration.
claims.source: Hence, overexpression of KITL in RPE does not play a major role in prevention of light-induced photoreceptor degeneration.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the TUNEL data showing only a slight reduction in photoreceptor cell death after AAV8-RPE65-KITL infection.

claims.claim: Infection with AAV8-RHO-KITL led to overexpression specifically in photoreceptor cells (increase over control by 4.23 ± 0.68 fold, n = 4).
claims.source: Infection with AAV8-RHO-KITL led to overexpression specifically in photoreceptor cells as shown by WB (increase over control by 4.23 ± 0.68 fold, n = 4) and IF (Figure 5G and H), confirming previous reports (Allocca et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 5G,H and a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells reduced the light damage-induced decrease of ONL thickness.
claims.source: In contrast to overexpression in RPE, however, overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells reduced the LD-induced decrease of ONL thickness (Figure 5I,J) and prevented photoreceptor cell death (from 25.9 ± 4.7%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RHO-Flag to 11.5 ± 2.5%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RHO-KITL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-b, C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 5I,J.

claims.claim: Overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells prevented photoreceptor cell death (from 25.9 ± 4.7%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RHO-Flag to 11.5 ± 2.5%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RHO-KITL).
claims.source: In contrast to overexpression in RPE, however, overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells reduced the LD-induced decrease of ONL thickness (Figure 5I,J) and prevented photoreceptor cell death (from 25.9 ± 4.7%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RHO-Flag to 11.5 ± 2.5%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RHO-KITL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-b, C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay images and quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-b, C.

claims.claim: Overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells protects these cells more efficiently than overexpression in RPE cells.
claims.source: Collectively, these results clearly indicate that overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells protects these cells more efficiently than overexpression in RPE cells, underscoring the cell-autonomous effect of KITL.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of protective effects between AAV8-RPE65-KITL and AAV8-RHO-KITL.

claims.claim: After light damage, the expression of 17 antioxidant and wound healing genes, including Axl and Hmox1, was changed in Kit+/+ retinas.
claims.source: In fact, after LD, the expression of 17 such genes, including Axl and Hmox1, was changed in Kit+/+ retinas (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the heat map shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: HMOX1 catalyzes the degradation of heme into three biologically active end products, biliverdin/bilirubin, CO and ferrous ion.
claims.source: The protein product of Hmox1, HMOX1, catalyzes the degradation of heme into three biologically active end products, biliverdin/bilirubin, CO and ferrous ion (Otterbein et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: HMOX1 is known to be induced by oxidative stress in multiple tissues as well as by light damage of the retina.
claims.source: It is known to be induced by oxidative stress in multiple tissues as well as by LD of the retina (Kutty et al., 1995) and thought to act as an antioxidant (Otterbein et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: HMOX1 is thought to act as an antioxidant.
claims.source: It is known to be induced by oxidative stress in multiple tissues as well as by LD of the retina (Kutty et al., 1995) and thought to act as an antioxidant (Otterbein et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Under normal light/dark cycle conditions, HMOX1 levels were similarly low in both Kit+/+ and KitWps/Wps retinas.
claims.source: Under normal light/dark cycle conditions, HMOX1 levels analyzed on western blots (Figure 6C) or by immunostaining (Figure 6D) were similarly low in both Kit+/+ and KitWps/Wps retinas.
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claims.claim: After light damage, HMOX1 expression was significantly upregulated in Kit+/+ retinas (3.6 ± 0.6 fold) but only slightly in KitWps/Wps retinas (1.4 ± 0.5 fold, n = 3).
claims.source: After LD, however, HMOX1 expression was significantly upregulated in Kit+/+ retinas (3.6 ± 0.6 fold) but only slightly in KitWps/Wps retinas (1.4 ± 0.5 fold, n = 3) (Figure 6C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claims.claim: Light damage-dependent upregulation of Hmox1 is markedly influenced by KIT signaling.
claims.source: These data indicate that LD-dependent upregulation of Hmox1 is markedly influenced by KIT signaling.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data showing differential HMOX1 upregulation between Kit+/+ and KitWps/Wps retinas after light damage.

claims.claim: Transfection with KIT led to upregulation of HMOX1, with a clear difference between KIT-WT (6.2 ± 0.86 fold, n = 4) and KIT-Wps (3 ± 0.6 fold, n = 4) in 661W cells.
claims.source: Transfection with KIT also led to upregulation of HMOX1, although with a clear difference between KIT-WT (6.2 ± 0.86 fold, n = 4) and KIT-Wps (3 ± 0.6 fold, n = 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: One week after injection of AAV8-KITL, western blots showed a correlation between high levels of KITL (4.6 ± 0.9 fold induction, n = 4) and HMOX1 (2.9 ± 0.5 fold induction, n = 4) in Kit+/+ mice kept under normal light conditions.
claims.source: One week after injection, western blots showed a correlation between high levels of KITL (4.6 ± 0.9 fold induction, n = 4) and HMOX1 (2.9 ± 0.5 fold induction, n = 4) (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Immunostaining showed that the expression of KITL was dramatically enhanced in the superior retinal region around the location of injection, coinciding with high level HMOX1 expression.
claims.source: Consistent with this observation, immunostaining showed that the expression of KITL was dramatically enhanced in the superior retinal region around the location of injection, coinciding with high level HMOX1 expression (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Activation of KIT signaling can induce HMOX1 expression in Kit+/+ retinas independent of light damage treatment.
claims.source: These data suggest that activation of KIT signaling can induce HMOX1 expression in Kit+/+ retinas independent of LD treatment.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data showing increased HMOX1 expression after AAV8-KITL injection in mice kept under normal light conditions.

claims.claim: Western blots showed no change in NRF2 expression in retinas after light treatment.
claims.source: Although western blots showed no change in NRF2 expression in retinas after light treatment (Figure 7A,B), immunostaining indicated a dramatic increase in nuclear accumulation of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells after light treatment for 8 days (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claims.claim: Immunostaining indicated a dramatic increase in nuclear accumulation of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells after light treatment for 8 days.
claims.source: Although western blots showed no change in NRF2 expression in retinas after light treatment (Figure 7A,B), immunostaining indicated a dramatic increase in nuclear accumulation of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells after light treatment for 8 days (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Nuclear accumulation of NRF2 was much reduced in KitWps/Wps mice (14 ± 5 per section, n = 6) compared to Kit+/+ mice (28 ± 9, n = 6) after light treatment.
claims.source: This nuclear accumulation was much reduced in KitWps/Wps mice (14 ± 5 per section, n = 6) compared to Kit+/+ mice (28 ± 9, n = 6) (Figure 7C,D), suggesting that Kit signaling regulates nuclear translocation of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images and quantification shown in Figure 7C,D.

claims.claim: Kit signaling regulates nuclear translocation of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells.
claims.source: This nuclear accumulation was much reduced in KitWps/Wps mice (14 ± 5 per section, n = 6) compared to Kit+/+ mice (28 ± 9, n = 6) (Figure 7C,D), suggesting that Kit signaling regulates nuclear translocation of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data showing differential nuclear accumulation of NRF2 between Kit+/+ and KitWps/Wps mice after light treatment.

claims.claim: Knockdown of Kitl increased the number of 661W cells with cytosolic NRF2 expression from 4.74 ± 2.27% to 30.2 ± 8.3% or 36.8 ± 2.24% (n = 3).
claims.source: Indeed, immunostaining revealed that both Kitl-si-RNAs increased the number of cells with cytosolic NRF2 expression from 4.74 ± 2.27% to 30.2 ± 8.3% or 36.8 ± 2.24% (n = 3), respectively (Figure 7E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images and quantification shown in Figure 7E,F.

claims.claim: Knock down of Kitl increased the levels of NRF2 in the cytoplasm (1.5 ± 0.13 fold, n = 3) and decreased the levels of nuclear NRF2 (0.59 ± 0.09 fold, n = 3) in 661W cells.
claims.source: In addition, western blots showed that knock down of Kitl increased the levels of NRF2 in the cytoplasm (1.5 ± 0.13 fold, n = 3) and decreased the levels of nuclear NRF2 (0.59 ± 0.09 fold, n = 3) (Figure 7G,H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7G,H.

claims.claim: KIT signaling regulates the cytoplasmic/nuclear distribution of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells.
claims.source: Taken together, these data clearly show that KIT signaling regulates the cytoplasmic/nuclear distribution of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on the immunostaining and western blot data showing effects of Kitl knockdown on NRF2 localization.

claims.claim: Overexpression of KIT upregulated Hmox1 expression (2.35 ± 1 fold, n = 3) in 661W cells.
claims.source: Consistently, overexpression of KIT did not significantly change Nfe2l2 expression (1.1 ± 0.2 fold, n = 3) but upregulated Hmox1 expression (2.35 ± 1 fold, n = 3). This upregulation was blocked by knockdown of Nfe2l2.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and qPCR data shown in Figure 7I,J.

claims.claim: Upregulation of Hmox1 by overexpression of KIT was blocked by knockdown of Nfe2l2 in 661W cells.
claims.source: Consistently, overexpression of KIT did not significantly change Nfe2l2 expression (1.1 ± 0.2 fold, n = 3) but upregulated Hmox1 expression (2.35 ± 1 fold, n = 3). This upregulation was blocked by knockdown of Nfe2l2.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and qPCR data shown in Figure 7I,J.

claims.claim: KIT signaling activates NRF2 to regulate the expression of Hmox1 in photoreceptor cells.
claims.source: Collectively, these data suggest that KIT signaling activates NRF2 to regulate the expression of Hmox1 in photoreceptor cells.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data showing that knockdown of Nfe2l2 blocks KIT-induced upregulation of Hmox1.

claims.claim: Western blotting and immunostaining showed photoreceptor-restricted expression of HMOX1 two weeks after AAV8-HMOX1 virus infection.
claims.source: Western blotting and immunostaining showed photoreceptor-restricted expression after 2 weeks after virus infection (Figure 8A,B), with levels similar to those observed in uninjected Kit+/+ retinas after LD.
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claims.claim: Without light damage, control AAV8 or AAV8-HMOX1 virus did not cause significant changes in the ERG scotopic trace in KitWps/Wps albino mice.
claims.source: ERG measurements showed that without LD, control AAV8 or AAV8-HMOX1 virus did not cause significant changes in the ERG scotopic trace (Figure 8C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ERG traces shown in Figure 8C,D.

claims.claim: Following 3 days of light damage, the b-wave amplitudes were higher when AAV8-HMOX1 was used (381 ± 40μV, n = 5) compared to when control AAV8 was used (152 ± 33 μV, n = 5) in KitWps/Wps albino mice.
claims.source: Following 3 days of LD, however, the amplitudes of ERG scotopic traces were depressed after infection with AAV8 or AAV8-HMOX1 virus, but the b-wave amplitudes were higher when AAV8-HMOX1 was used (381 ± 40μV, n = 5) compared to when control AAV8 was used (152 ± 33 μV, n = 5) (Figure 8C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ERG traces and quantification shown in Figure 8C,D.

claims.claim: Overexpression of HMOX1 partially rescues retinal function in the KitWps/Wps albino mice during light damage.
claims.source: These results suggest that overexpression of HMOX1 partially rescues retinal function in the KitWps/Wps albino mice during LD.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the ERG data showing improved b-wave amplitudes in AAV8-HMOX1 infected mice compared to control.

claims.claim: After light damage, AAV8-HMOX1-infected retinas were thicker than control AAV8-infected ones, especially with respect to the photoreceptor cell layer.
claims.source: Furthermore, histological analyses showed that after LD, AAV8-HMOX1-infected retinas were thicker than control AAV8-infected ones, especially with respect to the photoreceptor cell layer (Figure 8E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 8E,F.

claims.claim: Overexpression of HMOX1 protects photoreceptor cells in KitWps/Wps albino retinas against light damage.
claims.source: These data suggest that overexpression of HMOX1 protects photoreceptor cells in KitWps/Wps albino retinas against LD and that LD-induced HMOX1 plays an important antioxidant role in retinas in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the histological data showing increased retinal thickness in AAV8-HMOX1 infected mice after light damage.

claims.claim: Light damage-induced HMOX1 plays an important antioxidant role in retinas in vivo.
claims.source: These data suggest that overexpression of HMOX1 protects photoreceptor cells in KitWps/Wps albino retinas against LD and that LD-induced HMOX1 plays an important antioxidant role in retinas in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the protective effects of HMOX1 overexpression against light damage.

claims.claim: Addition of exogenous KITL (5.6 nM) was able to prevent cell loss caused by light damage in 661W cells (from 409 ± 44 to 147 ± 15 (n = 3) after 8 hr of LD treatment to 278 ± 28 (n = 3)).
claims.source: As shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D, cell numbers were similar in each group before LD but dramatically decreased in the control group (from 409 ± 44 to 147 ± 15 (n = 3) after 8 hr of LD treatment). Addition of exogenous KITL (5.6 nM) was able to prevent cell loss caused by LD to 278 ± 28 (n = 3). This preventive effect was totally blocked by knockdown of Hmox1 via Hmox1-si-RNAs (cell loss 147 ± 16, n = 3 and 131 ± 17, n = 3, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: The preventive effect of KITL on light-induced cell loss was totally blocked by knockdown of Hmox1 via Hmox1-si-RNAs in 661W cells.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D, cell numbers were similar in each group before LD but dramatically decreased in the control group (from 409 ± 44 to 147 ± 15 (n = 3) after 8 hr of LD treatment). Addition of exogenous KITL (5.6 nM) was able to prevent cell loss caused by LD to 278 ± 28 (n = 3). This preventive effect was totally blocked by knockdown of Hmox1 via Hmox1-si-RNAs (cell loss 147 ± 16, n = 3 and 131 ± 17, n = 3, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: Stimulation of KITL decreased light-induced cell death rate from 83 ± 4.6% to 40 ± 5.3% (n = 3) in 661W cells, but this protection by KITL disappeared when the expression of Hmox1 was knocked down by Hmox1-si-RNAs.
claims.source: In addition, the data of propidium iodide (PI) staining also showed that stimulation of KITL decreased light-induced cell death rate from 83 ± 4.6% to 40 ± 5.3% (n = 3), but this protection by KITL disappeared when the expression of Hmox1 was knocked down by Hmox1-si-RNAs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PI staining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Protection of KITL against light-induced photoreceptor cell loss depends on HMOX1.
claims.source: These results suggest that protection of KITL against light-induced photoreceptor cell loss depends on HMOX1.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that knockdown of Hmox1 blocks the protective effect of KITL in 661W cells.

claims.claim: Mice homozygous for a mutation in the gene encoding the photoreceptor cGMP phosphodiesterase, Pde6brd10, share many characteristics of human retinal degeneration resulting from a mutation in the homologous gene.
claims.source: Mice homozygous for a mutation in the gene encoding the photoreceptor cGMP phosphodiesterase, Pde6brd10 (hereafter called rd10/rd10) share many characteristics of human retinal degeneration resulting from a mutation in the homologous gene (Wang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Subretinal injection of AAV8-KITL virus at P3 can mediate overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells of rd10/rd10 mice.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 9A, ectopic expression of KITL was observed at 3 weeks in rd10/rd10 photoreceptor cells in the eye infected with AAV8-KITL, but not in those of the control-injected contralateral eye. These results suggest that subretinal injection of AAV8-KITL virus at P3 can mediate overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells of rd10/rd10 mice.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: The thickness of the ONL was significantly increased from the peripheral region to the central region after infection with the AAV8-KITL virus in rd10/rd10 mice.
claims.source: The thickness of the ONL was significantly increased from the peripheral region to the central region after infection with the AAV8-KITL virus (Figure 9B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 9B,C.

claims.claim: In P24 control-injected rd10/rd10 retina, Rhodopsin was abnormally translocated from the OS to the ONL, a phenomenon that was partially rescued by infection with the AAV8-KITL virus.

results.result: Photoreceptor degeneration is a major cause of blindness with limited treatment options. The authors establish the clinical context by noting that photoreceptor loss is common to multiple retinal degenerative diseases (cone dystrophy, RP, AMD), that RP involves mutations in ~80 genes with various inheritance patterns, and that despite recent gene therapy approval for RPE65 mutations, broadly applicable treatments remain unavailable.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1, C2, C16-C22) provide well-established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. They accurately describe the clinical significance of photoreceptor degeneration, the genetic complexity of RP, and the current limitations in treatment options. This contextual information is standard in the field and appropriately referenced.

results.result: Several neuroprotective factors (CNTF, GDNF, PEDF, RdCVF) have been identified but face clinical limitations. The authors note that while limited light stress activates protective pathways like FGF2/gp130, and prolonged light exposure upregulates CNTF and FGF2, these factors have short half-lives, systemic side effects, and reduced efficacy, with none commercially available for clinical use.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C29 accurately summarize prior work on neuroprotective factors and their limitations, all supported by appropriate citations. This establishes the rationale for seeking novel protective factors and validates the use of light damage as a discovery strategy.

results.result: KIT/KITL signaling is an important pathway in multiple cell types but its role in adult retina was unknown. The authors establish that KITL interacts with KIT receptor to promote cell survival, migration, and proliferation through MAPK, PI3K, JAK/STAT, and SRC pathways. While KIT is expressed in retinal progenitor cells, its functional role in adult retina had not been characterized prior to this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C38 provide well-documented background on KIT/KITL signaling from prior literature (C30-C36) and accurately identify the knowledge gap (C37-C38) that motivates the current study. All statements are appropriately cited.

results.result: Light damage induces molecular changes in the retina including upregulation of KITL. RNA-seq analysis after 1 day of light exposure (15,000 Lux) showed significant gene expression changes including known light-inducible genes (Gfap, Edn2, Fgf2, Ccl3, Ccl12) and identified the MAPK pathway among top altered pathways, with increased expression of Kitl, Lif, and Ngf confirmed by RT-PCR.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C49 are well-supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 1A-D), RT-PCR validation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and appropriate statistical thresholds (p<0.01, fold change >2). The identification of known light-inducible genes validates the approach, and the discovery of Kitl upregulation is clearly documented.

results.result: Photoreceptor cells are the major source of KITL upregulation following light stress. Western blots showed increased transmembrane (2.4±0.9 fold) and soluble (4.5±1.6 fold) KITL forms, and increased phosphorylated KIT (3.14±0.94 fold) after light damage. Multiple approaches (Q-PCR, western blot, in situ hybridization, immunostaining) demonstrated that Kitl expression is higher in neural retina compared to RPE under normal conditions and is upregulated in photoreceptors but not RPE after light damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C50-C57 are strongly supported by converging evidence from multiple complementary techniques (RNA-seq, RT-PCR, western blot, immunostaining, in situ hybridization) shown in Figure 1 and supplements. The quantitative data include appropriate replicates (n=3-5) and the cell-type specificity is well-documented through tissue separation experiments.

results.result: KitWps/Wps mice show normal retinal structure and function under baseline conditions. The KitWps mutation (D60N in extracellular domain) produces viable but white and infertile mice. Under normal conditions, these mice show no detectable changes in fundus appearance, ERG responses (scotopic or photopic), retinal histology, cell layer thickness, or expression of retinal cell markers (OTX2, PKCα, Rhodopsin, Opsin).
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C65 are well-supported by comprehensive baseline characterization in Figure 2A-G, including fundus imaging, ERG measurements, histology, and immunostaining with appropriate quantification. The data establish that the KitWps mutation does not cause developmental or baseline functional defects in the retina, which is critical for interpreting subsequent light damage experiments.

results.result: The KitWps mutation substantially reduces KIT activation in the retina. While the AB5506 antibody (recognizing intracellular domain) showed similar KIT expression between genotypes, the ACK45 antibody (recognizing extracellular domain) showed significantly decreased immunoreactivity in KitWps/Wps retinas. Intravitreal KITL injection induced phosphorylation of KIT, ERK, and AKT in Kit+/+ but not KitWps/Wps retinas.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by western blot and immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2H-J. The use of two different antibodies recognizing different epitopes provides strong evidence that the mutation affects ligand binding and receptor activation rather than expression levels. The functional validation through downstream signaling (ERK, AKT phosphorylation) is appropriate.

results.result: KitWps/Wps mice show exacerbated photoreceptor degeneration after light damage. Following 8 days of light exposure (15,000 lux), KitWps/Wps mice showed greater decline in ERG responses (both scotopic and photopic), more severe ONL thinning, increased reactive gliosis (GFAP), abnormal rhodopsin translocation, and higher photoreceptor cell death (44±9 vs 22±7 TUNEL+ cells per section) compared to Kit+/+ mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C82 are strongly supported by comprehensive functional and structural analyses in Figure 3, including ERG measurements (n=8 per group), histological quantification, immunostaining for multiple markers, and TUNEL assays (n=10 per group). The convergent evidence from multiple independent measures (function, structure, cell death) provides robust support for the conclusion that KIT signaling protects against light-induced degeneration.

results.result: AAV8-mediated KITL overexpression prevents light-induced photoreceptor degeneration in wild-type mice. AAV8-KITL infection achieved widespread retinal transduction with photoreceptor-specific expression (3.3±0.46 fold increase). Without light damage, AAV8-KITL caused no morphological changes. After 3 days of light damage, AAV8-KITL-infected retinas showed preserved thickness and dramatically reduced photoreceptor cell death (9±1.6% vs 40.8±4.5% with control AAV8).
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C91 are well-supported by data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 1-2, including validation of AAV8 transduction efficiency, western blot confirmation of KITL overexpression, histological analysis, and TUNEL assays with appropriate sample sizes (n=6 per group). The protective effect is substantial and statistically significant.

results.result: KITL protection against light damage requires functional KIT receptor. In albino mice after light damage, AAV8-KITL prevented retinal thinning and reduced photoreceptor cell death in Kit+/+ mice (from 40.6±8.2% to 8.9±2.1%) but not in KitWps/Wps mice (remained at 75.9±8.2%), demonstrating that KITL acts through KIT receptor activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 provide critical genetic evidence for mechanism in Figure 4H-J. The use of albino mice on both genetic backgrounds controls for the RPE65 variant, and the differential response to AAV8-KITL between genotypes (n=4 per group) strongly supports that protection requires functional KIT signaling. This is a well-designed experiment that rules out off-target effects.

results.result: KITL protection is cell-autonomous in photoreceptors. RPE-specific KITL expression (AAV8-RPE65-KITL, 12.1±2.4 fold increase) provided minimal protection (cell death 26.6±5% to 21.7±2.8%), while photoreceptor-specific expression (AAV8-RHO-KITL, 4.23±0.68 fold increase) significantly reduced ONL thinning and cell death (from 25.9±4.7% to 11.5±2.5%), demonstrating that photoreceptor-expressed KITL is more protective than RPE-expressed KITL.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C104 are supported by cell-type-specific AAV experiments in Figure 5, using validated promoters (RPE65 for RPE, RHO for photoreceptors) with western blot and immunostaining confirmation of expression patterns. The differential protective effects (n=8 per group) provide strong evidence for cell-autonomous action. This is an important mechanistic finding.

results.result: KIT signaling regulates HMOX1 expression in photoreceptors. RNA-seq identified 17 antioxidant/wound healing genes altered by light damage, including Hmox1. Under normal conditions, HMOX1 levels were similar between genotypes, but after light damage, HMOX1 was significantly upregulated in Kit+/+ retinas (3.6±0.6 fold) but only slightly in KitWps/Wps retinas (1.4±0.5 fold), indicating KIT-dependent regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C111 are supported by RNA-seq analysis (Figure 6A-B), western blots, and immunostaining (Figure 6C-D) with appropriate replicates (n=3). The differential HMOX1 induction between genotypes provides strong evidence for KIT-dependent regulation. The background on HMOX1 function (C106-C108) is appropriately cited.

results.result: KIT activation induces HMOX1 expression independent of light damage. In vitro, KIT-WT transfection increased HMOX1 more than KIT-Wps (6.2±0.86 vs 3±0.6 fold). In vivo, AAV8-KITL injection in Kit+/+ mice under normal light conditions increased both KITL (4.6±0.9 fold) and HMOX1 (2.9±0.5 fold), with colocalization in photoreceptors, demonstrating that KIT activation alone is sufficient to induce HMOX1.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C115 are supported by both in vitro (661W cells, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) and in vivo (AAV8-KITL injection, Figure 6E-F) experiments with appropriate controls and replicates (n=4). The convergent evidence from two experimental systems strengthens the conclusion that KIT directly regulates HMOX1 expression.

results.result: KIT signaling regulates nuclear translocation of NRF2. While total NRF2 levels were unchanged after light treatment, immunostaining showed dramatic increase in nuclear NRF2 in Kit+/+ photoreceptors (28±9 per section) but much less in KitWps/Wps (14±5 per section). In vitro, Kitl knockdown increased cytosolic NRF2 (from 4.74±2.27% to 30-37% of cells) and decreased nuclear NRF2 (0.59±0.09 fold), demonstrating KIT-dependent regulation of NRF2 localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C116-C122 are well-supported by immunostaining (Figure 7A-F) and western blot analysis of subcellular fractions (Figure 7G-H) with appropriate quantification and replicates (n=3-6). The use of both in vivo (genetic mutant) and in vitro (siRNA knockdown) approaches provides strong converging evidence for KIT regulation of NRF2 nuclear translocation.

results.result: KIT signaling stimulates Hmox1 expression through NRF2. In 661W cells, KIT overexpression upregulated Hmox1 (2.35±1 fold) without changing Nfe2l2 expression (1.1±0.2 fold), and this upregulation was blocked by Nfe2l2 knockdown, demonstrating that KIT activates NRF2 to regulate Hmox1 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C41, C123-C125 are supported by RT-PCR and qPCR data in Figure 7I-J showing that Nfe2l2 knockdown blocks KIT-induced Hmox1 upregulation (n=3). This establishes the epistatic relationship between KIT, NRF2, and HMOX1, completing the mechanistic pathway. The experimental design appropriately tests the requirement for NRF2.

results.result: HMOX1 overexpression rescues light-induced photoreceptor degeneration in KitWps/Wps mice. AAV8-HMOX1 achieved photoreceptor-specific expression at levels similar to light-damaged Kit+/+ retinas. In KitWps/Wps albino mice, AAV8-HMOX1 partially rescued ERG function after light damage (b-wave: 381±40μV vs 152±33μV with control) and preserved retinal thickness, demonstrating that HMOX1 acts downstream of KIT to protect photoreceptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C42, C126-C132 are supported by AAV8-HMOX1 rescue experiments in Figure 8A-F with appropriate controls, ERG measurements (n=5), and histological analysis (n=6). The partial rescue in KitWps/Wps mice by HMOX1 overexpression provides strong genetic evidence that HMOX1 is a key downstream effector of KIT signaling. This is a critical experiment establishing the mechanistic pathway.

results.result: KITL protection against light damage depends on HMOX1. In 661W cells, exogenous KITL (5.6 nM) prevented light-induced cell loss (from 409±44 to 278±28 cells vs 147±15 in control) and reduced cell death (from 83±4.6% to 40±5.3%), but this protection was completely blocked by Hmox1 knockdown, demonstrating that HMOX1 is required for KITL-mediated protection.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C136 are supported by in vitro experiments in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C-E using cell counting and PI staining (n=3). The complete loss of KITL protection upon Hmox1 knockdown provides strong evidence for the requirement of HMOX1. This complements the in vivo rescue experiments and establishes HMOX1 as a necessary downstream mediator.

results.result: KITL overexpression protects against inherited retinal degeneration in rd10 and rd1 mouse models. In rd10/rd10 mice (Pde6b mutation), subretinal AAV8-KITL injection at P3 achieved photoreceptor-specific KITL expression, significantly increased ONL thickness, partially rescued rhodopsin localization, reduced photoreceptor cell death (from 16.2±2% to 8.9±1.6%), and improved ERG responses (b-wave: 304±30μV vs 142.2±43.6μV), with similar results in rd1/rd1 mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C13, C14, C137-C144 are supported by comprehensive analysis in Figure 9 and Figure 9—figure supplement 1, including immunostaining, histology, TUNEL assays (n=5), and ERG measurements (n=5) in two independent genetic models of RP. The demonstration of protection in genetic models distinct from light damage provides strong evidence for broad therapeutic potential. This is a major translational finding.

results.result: KIT signaling protects photoreceptor cells against light-induced retinal degeneration through the NRF2-HMOX1 pathway. Multiple lines of evidence support that KIT is expressed in photoreceptor cells, its activation stimulates MAPK and PI3K/AKT pathways, KIT signaling activates NRF2 leading to HMOX1 expression, and this pathway protects against light-induced degeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C145-C147, C169 represent the integrated conclusion supported by the entire body of experimental evidence including: (1) KIT expression and activation in photoreceptors, (2) exacerbated degeneration in KitWps/Wps mice, (3) protection by KITL overexpression, (4) KIT-dependent NRF2 nuclear translocation, (5) NRF2-dependent HMOX1 expression, and (6) HMOX1-dependent protection. The mechanistic pathway is well-established through genetic, pharmacological, and molecular approaches.

results.result: KITL may provide a novel therapeutic avenue for retinal degenerative diseases. The authors conclude that given the protective effects in both light damage and genetic models, KITL/KIT signaling activation may be considered clinically for photoreceptor protection, potentially offering advantages over other strategies and working regardless of specific pathogenetic mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C12, C15, C148-C150, C170-C171 represent speculative therapeutic conclusions. While the mouse data are compelling, claim C12 (partial restoration of retinal function after light damage) lacks direct ERG evidence in the light damage + AAV8-KITL condition. The therapeutic potential claims (C15, C148, C170-C171) are reasonable extrapolations but remain speculative without human data or additional safety/efficacy studies. The comparison to other therapies (C149) and broad applicability claims require further validation.

results.result: KIT signaling activation should be used with caution due to potential tumorigenic effects, though local AAV-mediated expression may mitigate risks. The authors note that while KIT is needed for cell survival, excessive KIT signaling can lead to tumors (gastrointestinal stromal tumors, leukemia, melanoma), but suggest that local AAV-mediated expression with blood-retinal barrier protection may reduce deleterious effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C155 appropriately acknowledge known risks of KIT activation (C151-C153, supported by citation) and provide reasonable speculation about risk mitigation through local delivery (C154-C155). The cautionary note (C154) is appropriate given the known oncogenic potential, and the proposed mitigation strategy (C155) is plausible though speculative. This represents responsible discussion of translational considerations.

results.result: KITL acts cell-autonomously in photoreceptors through NRF2-mediated pathway. The authors establish that photoreceptor-specific KITL expression is more protective than RPE expression, that the pathway involves cytoplasm-to-nuclear shift of NRF2 likely mediated by AKT activation, and acknowledge potential indirect contributions from other cell types like Müller glia.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C159 are supported by the cell-type-specific AAV experiments (Figure 5) and mechanistic studies (Figure 7). The cell-autonomous conclusion (C156-C157) is well-supported by differential effects of RPE vs photoreceptor-specific expression. The mechanistic insight about AKT-mediated NRF2 translocation (C159) is supported by data and appropriate citation. The acknowledgment of potential indirect effects (C158) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: HMOX1 provides antioxidant protection in photoreceptors, and the KITL-KIT-NRF2-HMOX1 axis is one of multiple protective pathways. The authors note that HMOX1 reduces oxidative stress, that photoreceptors are particularly sensitive to oxidative damage, that oxidative stress is linked to AMD and other degenerations, and that KITL/HMOX1 overexpression provides only partial protection, suggesting multiple pathways are involved.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C168 appropriately contextualize the findings within oxidative stress biology (C160-C166, all well-cited) and acknowledge limitations (C167-C168). The observation that protection is partial rather than complete (C167, supported by data) leads to the reasonable conclusion that multiple pathways contribute to photoreceptor protection (C168). This represents appropriate scientific interpretation.
